say.text: A 52-year-old woman had total thyroidectomy and radioiodine for papillary cancer.
Which tumour marker do you follow for recurrence?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which cell the cancer came from, and which product that cell line makes. Then match the marker to the tumour's cell line.
Yes. After total thyroidectomy and radioiodine, thyroglobulin is the marker for recurrence, and a rising or detectable level suggests it.
It fits because differentiated cancer arises from follicular cells, the same cells that make thyroglobulin.

choices.label: I know this, skip the worked case

say.text: That choice is not right. It tempts because calcitonin is the thyroid tumour marker most often quoted in revision lists.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which tumour type raises this marker before you trust the list in your head.

say.text: Calcitonin is raised in medullary carcinoma, which comes from the C cells, and not in differentiated cancer.
After differentiated cancer surgery you follow thyroglobulin, the marker of the follicular-cell tumour.
That choice is not right. It tempts because CEA is a familiar tumour marker, and it sits beside calcitonin in medullary work-ups.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask which cell line this cancer came from before you choose its marker.

say.text: CEA is used alongside calcitonin for medullary carcinoma, the C-cell tumour.
Differentiated cancer is a follicular-cell cancer, and its follow-up marker is thyroglobulin.
Worked case, step by step. A 44-year-old had total thyroidectomy and radioiodine for papillary cancer. Two years on, her thyroglobulin is rising.
Step 1 is the marker. A rising thyroglobulin suggests recurrence, so the search starts. Step 2 is the assay. Her anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are negative, so the value counts.
Step 3 is the image. Neck ultrasound is clear, and the diagnostic whole-body iodine scan is negative, so no iodine-avid disease shows. Step 4 is the test left: FDG-PET finds iodine-negative disease.
A second patient, same follow-up: thyroglobulin is rising, antibodies are negative, neck ultrasound is clear, and the iodine scan is negative again.
What do you order next?

choices.label: Repeat the whole-body iodine scan, higher dose
Reassure, since a negative scan rules out recurrence
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the scan can see. It sees tumour that still takes up iodine. Which test sees tumour that does not?
Yes. A rising thyroglobulin with a negative iodine scan points to radioiodine-refractory disease, and FDG-PET finds tumour that has lost iodine uptake.
That choice is not right. It tempts because the iodine scan is the test you have just been taught to trust, and repeating it feels thorough.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the scan can see before you order it again.

say.text: A whole-body iodine scan detects only iodine-avid disease. A second negative scan has the same blind spot, so it cannot answer a rising marker.
The next test is the one that does not need iodine uptake: FDG-PET.
That choice is not right. It tempts because a negative scan feels like a clear result, and clear results usually end the worry.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask whether a rising marker still means something when the scan is clear.

say.text: A negative iodine scan does not exclude disease that has lost iodine uptake.
A rising thyroglobulin still flags recurrence, so the search continues with FDG-PET.
A third patient, five years after surgery. Her thyroglobulin is undetectable, but her anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are high.
How do you read the thyroglobulin?

choices.label: Undetectable, so no disease: routine follow-up
Undetectable settles it, whatever the antibodies
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether the assay itself can be trusted in a patient with these antibodies, before you read the number.
Yes. Antibodies spoil the thyroglobulin assay, so a low value cannot be trusted alone; you image the patient and follow the trend.
That choice is not right. It tempts because an undetectable value looks like a clean result, and clean results are what follow-up hopes for.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask first whether the thyroglobulin assay can be trusted in this patient.

say.text: Antibodies make the thyroglobulin assay unreliable, so an undetectable value can be false reassurance.
In an antibody-positive patient you image the neck and follow the trend, rather than act on one number.
That choice is not right. It tempts because a marker value feels like the decisive answer, and a single number is easy to act on.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what must be measured alongside thyroglobulin in this patient.

say.text: Thyroglobulin must be measured with its antibodies, because antibodies make the assay unreliable.
So no single value settles recurrence, and imaging is the check.
A patient had total thyroidectomy for medullary carcinoma.
Which marker do you follow after surgery?

choices.label: Thyroglobulin, as after any thyroid cancer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which cell line gave rise to this tumour, and which product that cell line secretes. Then match the marker to that product.
Yes. Medullary carcinoma comes from the C cells and raises calcitonin, so calcitonin with CEA tracks it.
That choice is not right. It tempts because thyroglobulin is the marker you have just learnt, and it feels like a rule for every thyroid cancer.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask which cell line this tumour came from before you choose its marker.

say.text: Thyroglobulin follows the follicular-cell cancers, papillary and follicular.
Medullary carcinoma comes from the C cells and is followed with calcitonin and CEA.
That choice is not right. It tempts because antibodies are tested alongside thyroglobulin, so the pairing looks like a standard panel.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether this tumour makes thyroglobulin at all.

say.text: The antibody pairing belongs to differentiated cancer, a follicular-cell cancer.
Medullary carcinoma is a C-cell tumour, followed with calcitonin and CEA.
Her thyroglobulin is rising, and her whole-body iodine scan is negative.
Which explanation fits the tumour?

choices.label: It still makes thyroglobulin but has lost iodine uptake
The scan is more sensitive, so the marker misleads
The tumour has turned medullary, so calcitonin rises
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the iodine scan needs the tumour to do, and whether a rising marker needs that same thing.
Yes. The tumour still makes thyroglobulin, so the marker rises, but it has lost iodine uptake, so the scan goes blind to it.
That choice is not right. It tempts because a scan picture feels more solid than a blood value, so it seems to overrule the marker.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask which test is blind to tumour that has lost iodine uptake.

say.text: The iodine scan sees only iodine-avid tissue, so a negative scan says nothing about iodine-negative cells.
Thyroglobulin still rises because the tumour still makes it. That is radioiodine-refractory disease.
That choice is not right. It tempts because two markers are in play, so a tumour that changes behaviour seems to change its marker.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask whether a differentiated cancer ever becomes a medullary one.

say.text: A differentiated cancer does not turn into a medullary carcinoma; they are separate tumours with separate markers.
The rising thyroglobulin is still the marker of the same follicular-cell tumour.
AJCC 8th edition staging of differentiated thyroid cancer uses an age cut-off.
What is the cut-off age, in years?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which edition's staging the stem means. Then ask which figure that edition used, not the one you remember from older papers.
Yes. The AJCC 8th edition uses 55 years as the cut-off for differentiated cancer staging.
Under that cut-off, stage I means no distant spread and stage II means distant spread.
That choice is not right. It tempts because the figure sits between the two editions you have met, so it feels like a blend of them.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask which edition this stem means before you give the number.

say.text: The AJCC 8th edition uses 55 years; the 7th edition used 45.
Older exam keys still say 45, so the number you remember may belong to a different edition.
That choice is not right. It tempts because 45 is the figure most revision notes and older papers still quote.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which edition the current staging uses.

say.text: PYQs have expected 45, the 7th edition figure. The current AJCC 8th edition uses 55.
Staging an under-55 patient follows the current cut-off, so check the edition first.
A 50-year-old woman has papillary carcinoma with lung metastasis.
Which AJCC 8th edition stage applies?

choices.label: Stage III, since she is over 45
Stage II, since under 55 with spread
Stage IVB, since distant spread is always IVB
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which edition's age cut-off applies to this patient, then ask what distant spread does at that age.
Yes. In the AJCC 8th edition, a patient younger than 55 with distant spread is stage II, not stage IV.
That choice is not right. It tempts because 45 is the old cut-off, and once it is in your head the age seems to decide the stage.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask which edition's cut-off this patient falls under.

say.text: The 45 figure belongs to the older edition.
Under the current 55 cut-off, distant spread in a patient under 55 is stage II.
That choice is not right. It tempts because distant spread is the feature staging weighs most, so stage IV feels inevitable.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the age cut-off changes the stage before you apply the spread.

say.text: Distant spread moves a patient into stage IV only at or over the cut-off.
Under 55, the same spread is stage II.
A surgeon in a hill-district clinic says follicular is now the most common differentiated thyroid cancer in his series.
What is the correct reply?

choices.label: Papillary leads overall; follicular's share rises here
Follicular is the commonest DTC in the hills
Follicular now outnumbers papillary across all regions
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether the stem asks for the overall leader or a share inside one region, before you name a cancer.
Yes. Papillary is the most common thyroid cancer overall, about 80 to 85 percent of cases.
Iodine deficiency raises follicular's share, which is a relative rise, not a change in the overall leader.
That choice is not right. It tempts because a clinic's own series feels like the national picture, so local experience seems typical.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask whether the stem wants the overall commonest cancer or a regional share.

say.text: Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer overall, about 80 to 85 percent of cases.
Follicular carcinoma's share rises in iodine-deficient areas, which is a regional change.
That choice is not right. It tempts because follicular carcinoma is the cancer iodine deficiency is linked to, so it seems to take over the whole picture.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the stem asks for the overall answer or a regional share.

say.text: Iodine deficiency is associated with follicular carcinoma, but that changes the share, not the overall leader.
Papillary stays the most common differentiated cancer in general series.
